postmortem.what_happened: Filled at a PTAX of 5.8889 on 19 Nov, already about 1.35% above the 18 Nov level the thesis cited; the central bank's US$1bn spot sale on 19 Nov reversed the same day and the real kept weakening on fiscal doubts, reaching 5.9708 on 23 Nov, when a later C08 review flipped the side and closed the position after three sessions.
postmortem.assessment: Over three sessions of a 20-day question the outcome is mostly noise, and the overshoot-fade view at 51% was defensible: in the December 2024 precedent the central bank escalated after early sales failed and the real recovered within weeks. The judgement weakness was ignoring that one named catalyst (the fiscal-package vote and the first auction) had fired and failed before the fill, and that much of the overshoot had moved before the fill mark. Graded on the same standard as J027, it is mixed, not a clear skill failure.
postmortem.do_differently: 1) Before fading an EM sell-off, state what would anchor the currency (heavier intervention, a credible finance minister, a fiscal vote) and whether it is likely inside the window. 2) Account for the gap between the decision-day level and the next-day fill. 3) Do not flip one-point leans day to day; grade near-50 positions by one consistent standard.

opposition.case_against: The draft judges the same three-session hold by a different standard than J027. J027's 49% lean losing over three days is 'noise'. J033's 51% lean losing over three days is a 'judgement error'. A 1.4% move in USD/BRL at this volatility is under one 3-day sigma, and the 20-day window from 18 Nov runs to mid-December, so 'thesis_right: no' is premature. The asymmetry looks like outcome bias driven by a vivid narrative. The case for 'no' is real: the Senate finished voting on the fiscal package on 19 Nov, the market judged it insufficient, and the $1bn spot sale reversed the same day, so one named catalyst fired and failed. The lesson is still the wrong one. 'Treat a failed intervention as a momentum signal' and 'don't fade before an anchor' are the rules that would have been most wrong in the closest precedent, December 2024. Then the BCB's early interventions also failed, it kept going (about $27.8bn within days), and USD/BRL fell back from above 6.0 into the high-5s within roughly 20 to 30 trading days. By 19 Nov the dollar was up about 7.8% in November and more than 17% since the eve of the run-off. An overshoot fade at 51% was a defensible view, if tiny, not a skill failure. Two of the draft's drivers turned up in no search: 'uncertainty over the next finance minister' and 'foreign buying of dollar futures'. One cited fact is off: the dollar index was described as at its strongest since March 2025, while 16 Nov coverage says its highest close since April 2025.
key_risks: Grading two identical near-50 short holds by different standards (luck vs judgement error) adds outcome bias to the post-mortem record
'thesis_right: no' at day 3 of a 20-day horizon may flip by mid-December if the Chamber vote or heavier BCB action anchors the real, as in Dec 2024
The 'failed intervention = momentum' heuristic rests on one episode and is contradicted by the 2024 precedent, where intervention escalated
Drivers in the draft (finance-minister uncertainty, foreign futures buying) are unverified and may be invented narrative
The decision-to-fill gap (5.8102 to 5.8889, about 1.35%) is not discussed; part of the 'overshoot' had already been absorbed at fill, which bears on the entry rule rather than the view
Dollar-index date claim (March 2025) conflicts with reporting of the highest close since April 2025
